Tutorial 9: Forecasting Distillation Dynamics with Long Short-Term Memory Networks

CHEE4003: Special Topics A - Artificial Intelligence in Chemical Engineering

Published

September 25, 2026

Forecasting a dynamic process

In previous tutorials, machine learning models were trained using independent observations, where each prediction depended only on the current input values. However, many chemical processes are dynamic, meaning that future process behaviour depends on both current conditions and past operating history.

One example is a binary distillation column. As shown in Figure 1, changes in heating input affect vapour generation and the separation of material throughout the column. Consequently, boilup and product compositions depend on both current operating conditions and the state of the column built up over time.

To model this time-dependent behaviour, we will use a long short-term memory (LSTM) network. Unlike the neural network models explored in previous tutorials, LSTMs are designed to learn from sequential data and maintain information about previous observations. This makes them well suited for dynamic processes, where future behaviour depends on past operating history.

The dataset contains 3,000 equally spaced measurements collected over 24 hours from the simulated binary distillation process shown in Figure 1. Heating input is the operating signal. Boilup, distillate composition, and reboiler liquid composition are measured responses. We use the reboiler composition as the dataset’s measure of bottoms composition; the CSV does not contain a separate bottoms-product measurement. Feed-tray composition is an additional measured state that can help predict those responses.

Below is a description of each of the variables in the dataset:

Column Role in this tutorial Engineering interpretation
Time (h) Time index Time since the beginning of the simulation
Heating Input (kJ/h) History feature Energy supplied to the reboiler; the operating signal
Boilup (mol/h) History feature and target Vapour generated in the column
Reboiler Composition History feature and target Reboiler liquid composition, used here for bottoms composition
Distillate Composition History feature and target Top-product composition
Feed Tray Composition History feature Internal composition that informs the forecast

In this tutorial, the recent history of all five measurements provides information about both the operating conditions and the internal state of the column. The model forecasts future boilup, bottoms composition (the Reboiler Composition column), and distillate composition. Past values of a target may appear in the history window; only future values are used as targets.

The tutorial has two parts. First, we construct and assess a one-step-ahead, multi-output LSTM. It receives the preceding 60 measurements, approximately 29 minutes of operation, and predicts the next boilup, bottoms composition, and distillate composition. Second, we extend the same idea to a direct multi-horizon, multi-output forecaster that predicts the next 50 values of all three targets, approximately 25 minutes, in one calculation. Unlike recursive forecasting, the direct forecaster does not feed its predictions back into the model. Instead, it is trained to predict all 150 future target values together.

The core activities are designed for approximately two hours.

NoteLearning objectives

After completing this tutorial, you will be able to:

  1. distinguish a dynamic process-forecasting problem from static regression;
  2. create chronological train, validation, and test periods without leaking future observations into training;
  3. transform process measurements into LSTM history windows and direct multi-horizon targets;
  4. construct an LSTM cell from nn.Linear, sigmoid, tanh, and tensor operations;
  5. train a one-step-ahead LSTM and inspect its predictions across the full training and test periods;
  6. extend the LSTM to forecast 50 future measurements of boilup and both product compositions in one forward pass; and
  7. join direct multi-output forecasts to their observed histories and compare horizon-wise error with a persistence baseline.

Next, use the load_distillation_data() function provided below to load the distillation dataset and perform a series of validation checks. The function confirms that all required columns are present, verifies that no missing values exist, and ensures that the measurements are ordered correctly in time.


load_distillation_data.py
def load_distillation_data(file_path):
    """Load time-ordered distillation data and validate required columns."""
    data = pd.read_csv(file_path)
    required_columns = [TIME_COLUMN, *FEATURE_COLUMNS]
    missing_columns = set(required_columns).difference(data.columns)
    if missing_columns:
        raise ValueError(f"Missing columns: {sorted(missing_columns)}")
    if data[required_columns].isna().any().any():
        raise ValueError("The tutorial data must not contain missing values.")
    if not data[TIME_COLUMN].is_monotonic_increasing:
        raise ValueError("Time values must be in increasing order.")
    return data

To better understand the behaviour of the distillation process, we will first visualise each variable as a function of time. The following function plots the operating signal and measured responses over the 24-hour simulation period.


plot_process_history.py
def plot_process_history(data):
    """Plot the operating signal and measured responses against time."""
    figure, axes = plt.subplots(5, 1, figsize=(8, 11), sharex=True)
    variables = FEATURE_COLUMNS
    colours = ["tab:orange", "tab:blue", "tab:green", "tab:red", "tab:purple"]
    for axis, variable, colour in zip(axes, variables, colours):
        axis.plot(data[TIME_COLUMN], data[variable], color=colour, linewidth=1)
        axis.set_ylabel(variable)
        axis.grid(alpha=0.3)
    axes[-1].set_xlabel("Time (h)")
    figure.suptitle("Distillation Operating Signal and Measured Responses", y=0.99)
    figure.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

From time series to supervised learning data

Considering that observations in a time series cannot be treated as independent samples. To train an LSTM, the process history must first be reorganised into input sequences and corresponding forecasting targets. An LSTM expects a sequence rather than one independent row at a time. For a forecast beginning at time \(t\), the input is a history window

\[ \mathbf{X}_t = [\mathbf{x}_{t-L}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{t-1}], \]

where \(L=60\) is the lookback length.

NoteLookback Window

  LSTMs do not receive a single observation as input. Instead, they are provided with a sequence of recent measurements called a lookback window. In this tutorial, each prediction uses the previous 60 measurements, corresponding to approximately 29 minutes of process history.

The target is a matrix of future boilup and product-composition measurements:

\[ \mathbf{Y}_t = \begin{bmatrix} V(t) & x_B(t) & x_D(t) \\ V(t+1) & x_B(t+1) & x_D(t+1) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ V(t+H-1) & x_B(t+H-1) & x_D(t+H-1) \end{bmatrix}, \]

where \(V\) is boilup in mol/h, \(x_B\) is the reboiler liquid composition, \(x_D\) is distillate composition, and \(H=50\) is the forecast horizon. The forecasting task therefore maps an input tensor with shape (batch, 60, 5) to an output tensor with shape (batch, 50, 3).

ImportantAvoid Data Leakage

Because the order of observations contains important information, the raw time series should not be randomly shuffled before splitting. Instead, the first 70% of observations are used for training, the next 15% for validation, and the final 15% for testing.

Randomly splitting generated windows would place overlapping histories and targets in different partitions, leading to unrealistically optimistic estimates of model performance. Any scaling transformations must therefore be fitted using only the training data to prevent future information from leaking into the preprocessing step.

The following functions perform the preprocessing required for time-series forecasting. They create chronological training, validation, and testing partitions, fit a standardisation transformation using only the training data, and apply the resulting scaling to the full dataset. Standardising each variable prevents boilup’s larger numerical units from dominating the training loss. Later, we calculate RMSE separately for each target in its original units.


chronological_boundaries.py
def chronological_boundaries(n_rows, train_fraction=0.70,
                             validation_fraction=0.15):
    """Return exclusive end indices for chronological data partitions."""
    if not 0 < train_fraction < 1:
        raise ValueError("train_fraction must be between 0 and 1.")
    if not 0 < validation_fraction < 1 - train_fraction:
        raise ValueError("validation_fraction must leave a test period.")
    train_end = int(n_rows * train_fraction)
    validation_end = train_end + int(n_rows * validation_fraction)
    return train_end, validation_end


def fit_standardizer(training_values):
    """Return feature-wise statistics fitted only to training data."""
    mean = training_values.mean(axis=0)
    standard_deviation = training_values.std(axis=0)
    if np.any(standard_deviation == 0):
        raise ValueError("A constant feature cannot be standardised.")
    return mean, standard_deviation


def standardize(values, mean, standard_deviation):
    """Apply supplied training-period statistics to an array."""
    return (values - mean) / standard_deviation

Use the functions defined above to create the chronological data partitions and standardise the process variables.

...
feature_values[:train_end])
>>>

...
feature_values, feature_mean, feature_standard_deviation).astype(np.float32)
>>>

>>>
target_mean = feature_mean[TARGET_FEATURE_INDICES]
>>>

>>>

)
>>>
np.testing.assert_allclose(
...
scaled_feature_values[:train_end].mean(axis=0),
...
np.zeros(len(FEATURE_COLUMNS)), atol=1e-5)

The assertions verify that the expected training and validation boundaries have been created and that the training data have been centred correctly after standardisation.

Task 1 : Create direct multi-horizon sequences

Write make_direct_horizon_windows. For every valid forecast start, it must return a history window of lookback feature rows, a matrix containing the next horizon scaled values for every target, and the integer index at which that target matrix begins.

TipImplementation guidance

The first history window is features[0:lookback]. Its target matrix begins immediately afterwards at target[lookback:lookback + horizon]. For every later window, move both slices forward by one row. There are len(features) - lookback - horizon + 1 complete windows.


make_direct_horizon_windows.py
def make_direct_horizon_windows(features, target, lookback, horizon):
    """
    Convert sequential features and multiple targets into direct forecast examples.

    Parameters
    ----------
    features : np.ndarray
        Array with shape ``(time, n_features)``.
    target : np.ndarray
        Array with shape ``(time, n_targets)`` containing scaled targets.
    lookback : int
        Number of prior rows in each history window.
    horizon : int
        Number of future target values predicted by each example.

    Returns
    -------
    X : torch.Tensor
        History windows with shape ``(examples, lookback, n_features)``.
    y : torch.Tensor
        Forecast targets with shape ``(examples, horizon, n_targets)``.
    forecast_starts : np.ndarray
        Index of the first target value for each example.
    """
>>>
X_all, y_all, forecast_starts = make_direct_horizon_windows(
...
scaled_feature_values, scaled_target_values, LOOKBACK, HORIZON
...
)
>>>
train_mask = forecast_starts + HORIZON <= train_end
>>>
validation_mask = ((forecast_starts >= train_end)
...
& (forecast_starts + HORIZON <= validation_end))
>>>
test_mask = forecast_starts >= validation_end
>>>
X_train, y_train = X_all[train_mask], y_all[train_mask]
>>>
X_validation, y_validation = X_all[validation_mask], y_all[validation_mask]
>>>
X_test, y_test = X_all[test_mask], y_all[test_mask]
>>>
print(f"Training windows: {len(X_train):,}")
 
Training windows: 1,991
>>>
print(f"Validation windows: {len(X_validation):,}")
 
Validation windows: 401
>>>
print(f"Test windows: {len(X_test):,}")
 
Test windows: 401
>>>
print(f"Input shape: {tuple(X_train.shape[1:])}")
 
Input shape: (60, 5)
>>>
print(f"Target shape: {tuple(y_train.shape[1:])}")
 
Target shape: (50, 3)
Callout-answerAnswer 

make_direct_horizon_windows.py
def make_direct_horizon_windows(features, target, lookback, horizon):
    if features.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("features must have shape (time, n_features).")
    if target.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("target must have shape (time, n_targets).")
    if len(features) != len(target):
        raise ValueError("features and target must have the same length.")
    if lookback < 1 or horizon < 1:
        raise ValueError("lookback and horizon must be positive integers.")

    n_windows = len(features) - lookback - horizon + 1
    if n_windows < 1:
        raise ValueError("The series is too short for this window and horizon.")

    X = np.empty((n_windows, lookback, features.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
    y = np.empty((n_windows, horizon, target.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
    forecast_starts = np.empty(n_windows, dtype=int)
    for window_index in range(n_windows):
        target_start = window_index + lookback
        X[window_index] = features[window_index:target_start]
        y[window_index] = target[target_start:target_start + horizon]
        forecast_starts[window_index] = target_start

    return torch.from_numpy(X), torch.from_numpy(y), forecast_starts

The historical measurements immediately before a validation or test forecast are realistic information: they would already be known when a forecast is issued. The target values themselves remain entirely within their assigned period.


make_loader.py
def make_loader(features, target, batch_size, shuffle):
    """Create a PyTorch data loader from forecast features and targets."""
    return DataLoader(TensorDataset(features, target), batch_size=batch_size,
                      shuffle=shuffle)


BATCH_SIZE = 128
train_loader = make_loader(X_train, y_train, BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True)
validation_loader = make_loader(X_validation, y_validation, BATCH_SIZE,
                                shuffle=False)
test_loader = make_loader(X_test, y_test, BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=False)

The completed training windows can and should be shuffled each epoch. TensorDataset keeps every history window paired with its own 50-by-3 forecast target while DataLoader(..., shuffle=True) changes only the order in which complete training examples are presented. Validation and test windows remain ordered.

Constructing an LSTM from basic neural-network blocks

PyTorch provides the optimised nn.LSTM module. In this tutorial, however, we will construct one LSTM cell directly from basic nn building blocks. This makes the information flow visible while PyTorch autograd still calculates the gradients required for training.

At every time step, the LSTM receives the current feature vector \(\mathbf{x}_t\), previous hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}\), and previous cell state \(\mathbf{c}_{t-1}\). A linear layer produces four gate vectors:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{i}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}] + \mathbf{b})_i, \\ \mathbf{f}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}] + \mathbf{b})_f, \\ \mathbf{g}_t &= \tanh(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}] + \mathbf{b})_g, \\ \mathbf{o}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}] + \mathbf{b})_o, \\ \mathbf{c}_t &= \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \mathbf{g}_t, \\ \mathbf{h}_t &= \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{c}_t). \end{aligned} \]

The input, forget, and output gates use the sigmoid function and therefore take values between zero and one. The candidate state uses tanh and takes values between negative one and one. The notation [x, h] means concatenation, so one linear layer with 4 * hidden_size outputs can calculate all four pre-activation gate vectors.

Task 2 : Build one manual LSTM cell

Complete ManualLSTMCell.forward. Concatenate the input and previous hidden state, apply self.gate_layer, split the result into input, forget, candidate, and output gates, then calculate the next cell and hidden states using the equations above.


manual_lstm_cell.py
class ManualLSTMCell(nn.Module):
    """One LSTM cell built from a linear layer and element-wise operations."""

    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.gate_layer = nn.Linear(
            input_size + hidden_size, 4 * hidden_size
        )

    def forward(self, x_t, h_previous, c_previous):
        """
        Update one LSTM state for a batch of current input vectors.

        Returns updated hidden and cell states, each with shape
        ``(batch, hidden_size)``.
        """
>>>
manual_cell = ManualLSTMCell(input_size=len(FEATURE_COLUMNS), hidden_size=8)
>>>
next_hidden, next_state = manual_cell(
...
torch.randn(4, len(FEATURE_COLUMNS)), torch.zeros(4, 8), torch.zeros(4, 8)
...
)
>>>
print(f"Manual LSTM hidden-state shape: {tuple(next_hidden.shape)}")
 
Manual LSTM hidden-state shape: (4, 8)
>>>
print(f"Manual LSTM cell-state shape: {tuple(next_state.shape)}")
 
Manual LSTM cell-state shape: (4, 8)
Callout-answerAnswer 

manual_lstm_cell.py
class ManualLSTMCell(nn.Module):
    """One LSTM cell built from a linear layer and element-wise operations."""

    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.gate_layer = nn.Linear(
            input_size + hidden_size, 4 * hidden_size
        )

    def forward(self, x_t, h_previous, c_previous):
        combined = torch.cat((x_t, h_previous), dim=1)
        input_gate, forget_gate, candidate_gate, output_gate = (
            self.gate_layer(combined).chunk(4, dim=1)
        )
        input_gate = torch.sigmoid(input_gate)
        forget_gate = torch.sigmoid(forget_gate)
        candidate_gate = torch.tanh(candidate_gate)
        output_gate = torch.sigmoid(output_gate)
        c_next = forget_gate * c_previous + input_gate * candidate_gate
        h_next = output_gate * torch.tanh(c_next)
        return h_next, c_next

Part 1: One-step-ahead LSTM forecasting

The first model predicts only the next measurement of each target. This is a one-step-ahead forecast: every history window of 60 measurements maps to one three-value target vector. It gives one unambiguous prediction for each forecast time, so we can plot predictions against observations across the complete training and test periods.

Prepare one-step examples

make_direct_horizon_windows already accepts a horizon length. Setting horizon=1 constructs one-step examples, then removing the length-one horizon dimension gives targets with shape (examples, 3).


prepare_one_step_examples.py

    make_direct_horizon_windows(
        scaled_feature_values, scaled_target_values, LOOKBACK, ONE_STEP_HORIZON
    )
)
y_one_step_all = y_one_step_all[:, 0, :]
one_step_train_mask = one_step_forecast_starts + ONE_STEP_HORIZON <= train_end

    (one_step_forecast_starts >= train_end)
    & (one_step_forecast_starts + ONE_STEP_HORIZON <= validation_end)

one_step_test_mask = one_step_forecast_starts >= validation_end

y_one_step_train = y_one_step_all[one_step_train_mask]
X_one_step_validation = X_one_step_all[one_step_validation_mask]
y_one_step_validation = y_one_step_all[one_step_validation_mask]

A one-step multi-output LSTM

The encoder is the same manual LSTM cell used above. Its output head has three units: one prediction each for boilup, bottoms composition, and distillate composition at the next measurement time.

Task 3 : Build the one-step LSTM

Complete OneStepLSTM.forward. Begin with zero hidden and cell states for the current batch. Apply self.cell to each time step of sequence, then use self.output_head to convert the final hidden state into the next three target predictions.


one_step_lstm.py
class OneStepLSTM(nn.Module):
    """Manual LSTM encoder followed by a one-step target output head."""

    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, target_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.cell = ManualLSTMCell(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.output_head = nn.Linear(hidden_size, target_size)

    def forward(self, sequence):
        """Return the next target vector with shape ``(batch, target_size)``."""
>>>
one_step_shape_model = OneStepLSTM(
...
input_size=len(FEATURE_COLUMNS), hidden_size=16,
...
target_size=len(TARGET_COLUMNS)
...
)
>>>
one_step_shape_forecast = one_step_shape_model(
...
torch.randn(5, LOOKBACK, len(FEATURE_COLUMNS))
...
)
Callout-answerAnswer 

one_step_lstm.py
class OneStepLSTM(nn.Module):
    """Manual LSTM encoder followed by a one-step target output head."""

    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, target_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.cell = ManualLSTMCell(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.output_head = nn.Linear(hidden_size, target_size)

    def forward(self, sequence):
        batch_size = sequence.shape[0]
        h_current = sequence.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        c_current = sequence.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        for time_step in range(sequence.shape[1]):
            h_current, c_current = self.cell(
                sequence[:, time_step, :], h_current, c_current
            )
        return self.output_head(h_current)

Train and assess the one-step LSTM

The same MSE training loop works for a one-step target matrix (batch, 3) and for the later direct multi-horizon target matrix (batch, 50, 3).


evaluate_loss.py
def evaluate_loss(model, data_loader, loss_function, device):
    """Return the mean loss over a data loader without calculating gradients."""
    model.eval()
    total_loss = 0.0
    total_examples = 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for feature_batch, target_batch in data_loader:
            feature_batch = feature_batch.to(device)
            target_batch = target_batch.to(device)
            batch_loss = loss_function(model(feature_batch), target_batch)
            total_loss += batch_loss.item() * len(feature_batch)
            total_examples += len(feature_batch)
    return total_loss / total_examples

Task 4 : Train an LSTM forecaster

Write train_model. For each epoch, set the model to training mode, move each batch to device, calculate its forecast and MSE loss, clear old gradients, backpropagate, and update the optimiser. After the training batches, calculate and store the validation loss.


train_model.py
def train_model(model, train_loader, validation_loader, device,
                epochs=40, learning_rate=3e-3):
    """Train an LSTM forecaster and return its training history."""
Callout-answerAnswer 

train_model.py
def train_model(model, train_loader, validation_loader, device,
                epochs=40, learning_rate=3e-3):
    loss_function = nn.MSELoss()
    optimiser = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
    history = {"train_loss": [], "validation_loss": []}
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        total_loss = 0.0
        total_examples = 0
        for feature_batch, target_batch in train_loader:
            feature_batch = feature_batch.to(device)
            target_batch = target_batch.to(device)
            optimiser.zero_grad()
            loss = loss_function(model(feature_batch), target_batch)
            loss.backward()
            optimiser.step()
            total_loss += loss.item() * len(feature_batch)
            total_examples += len(feature_batch)
        train_loss = total_loss / total_examples
        validation_loss = evaluate_loss(
            model, validation_loader, loss_function, device
        )
        history["train_loss"].append(train_loss)
        history["validation_loss"].append(validation_loss)
        if (epoch + 1) % 10 == 0 or epoch == 0:
            print(
                f"Epoch {epoch + 1:2d}/{epochs}: "
                f"train MSE = {train_loss:.5f}, "
                f"validation MSE = {validation_loss:.5f}"
            )
    return history

plot_training_history.py
def plot_training_history(history, title):
    """Plot training and validation MSE across model-training epochs."""
    epochs = np.arange(1, len(history["train_loss"]) + 1)
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.plot(epochs, history["train_loss"], label="Training MSE")
    plt.plot(epochs, history["validation_loss"], label="Validation MSE")
    plt.xlabel("Epoch")
    plt.ylabel("Scaled mean squared error")
    plt.title(title)
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


@torch.no_grad()
def predict(model, feature_tensor, device):
    """Return model forecasts on the CPU without tracking gradients."""
    model.eval()
    return model(feature_tensor.to(device)).cpu().numpy()


def inverse_target_scale(values, mean, standard_deviation):
    """Convert scaled target values back to their original units."""
    return values * standard_deviation + mean

Part 2: Direct multi-step LSTM forecasting

The one-step model makes one next-time prediction per history window. We now keep the same manual encoder but change its output head and targets so that each window produces a complete 50-step future trajectory in one forward pass.

A direct multi-horizon LSTM forecaster

The cell above processes one time step. The forecasting model repeatedly applies the same cell to all 60 rows in one history window. The final hidden state summarises the recent process history. A linear output head converts that state into all 50 future values for each of the three targets at once.

This is a sequence-to-matrix architecture. It is direct because the output head produces every forecasted value in one call. The 150 predicted values are not passed back into the LSTM.

Task 5 : Build the direct multi-horizon model

Complete DirectHorizonLSTM.forward. Begin with zero hidden and cell states for the current batch. Apply self.cell to each time step of sequence, then use self.forecast_head to convert the final hidden state into the forecast matrix.


direct_horizon_lstm.py
class DirectHorizonLSTM(nn.Module):
    """Manual LSTM encoder followed by a direct multi-horizon output head."""

    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, horizon, target_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.horizon = horizon
        self.target_size = target_size
        self.cell = ManualLSTMCell(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.forecast_head = nn.Linear(hidden_size, horizon * target_size)

    def forward(self, sequence):
        """
        Forecast a complete future horizon from a batch of history windows.

        ``sequence`` has shape ``(batch, lookback, input_size)`` and the
        returned tensor must have shape ``(batch, horizon, target_size)``.
        """

direct_horizon_lstm.py
class DirectHorizonLSTM(nn.Module):
    """Manual LSTM encoder followed by a direct multi-horizon output head."""

    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, horizon, target_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.horizon = horizon
        self.target_size = target_size
        self.cell = ManualLSTMCell(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.forecast_head = nn.Linear(hidden_size, horizon * target_size)

    def forward(self, sequence):
        batch_size = sequence.shape[0]
        h_current = sequence.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        c_current = sequence.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        for time_step in range(sequence.shape[1]):
            h_current, c_current = self.cell(
                sequence[:, time_step, :], h_current, c_current
            )
        forecast = self.forecast_head(h_current)
        return forecast.reshape(batch_size, self.horizon, self.target_size)

Evaluating direct multi-output forecasts

The network predicts standardised values for boilup and both compositions because that is the scale used for training. We convert each target back to its original units before calculating engineering metrics and plotting forecasts. Boilup RMSE is in mol/h, while composition RMSE is in composition units; compare each target with its own persistence baseline rather than comparing RMSE magnitudes across targets.

A useful baseline is persistence: repeat the final measured value of each target for every point in the future horizon. A dynamic LSTM is useful only if it improves on this transparent assumption for the intended forecast horizon.

Task 6 : Calculate horizon-wise RMSE

Write horizon_rmse. It should return one root mean squared error for every forecast position and every target. The first row measures one-sample-ahead error, while the final row measures error at the full 50-sample horizon.


horizon_rmse.py
def horizon_rmse(actual, predicted):
    """
    Calculate RMSE independently at every forecast position.

    Parameters
    ----------
    actual, predicted : np.ndarray
        Arrays with the common shape ``(forecasts, horizon, n_targets)``.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        RMSE values with shape ``(horizon, n_targets)``.
    """
Callout-answerAnswer 

horizon_rmse.py
def horizon_rmse(actual, predicted):
    if actual.shape != predicted.shape:
        raise ValueError("actual and predicted arrays must have the same shape.")
    if actual.ndim != 3:
        raise ValueError("actual and predicted arrays must be three-dimensional.")
    return np.sqrt(np.mean((actual - predicted) ** 2, axis=0))

Task 7 : Plot the multi-output forecast, input history, and actual outputs

A direct forecast is easier to interpret when the 50 predicted values for every target are drawn after the observed target history that the LSTM received and alongside the actual held-out outputs. Write plot_joined_forecast. The function receives the LOOKBACK observed time points and target matrix, plus the 50 forecast_times, 50-by-3 actual_values, and 50-by-3 forecast_values. It must use np.concatenate to create joined actual and predicted matrices, then plot actual and predicted trajectories in one subplot per target.

TipImplementation guidance

For a forecast that begins at row forecast_start, the history is time_values[forecast_start - LOOKBACK:forecast_start]. The forecast time points are time_values[forecast_start:forecast_start + HORIZON]. Use np.concatenate once with actual_values and once with forecast_values. Loop over target_names to create one subplot for boilup, bottoms composition, and distillate composition. In each subplot, draw the joined actual trajectory in black and the joined LSTM trajectory in a second colour. A vertical line at forecast_times[0] makes the change from observation to prediction clear.


plot_joined_forecast.py
def plot_joined_forecast(history_times, history_values, forecast_times,
                         actual_values, forecast_values, target_names):
    """Plot all direct forecasts against their histories and actual outputs.

    `forecast_times`, `actual_values`, and `forecast_values` must each contain
    the 50 points in the direct forecast horizon. The two value arrays have one
    column per target. Return the joined time, actual, and
    predicted target arrays after plotting them.
    """
Callout-answerAnswer 

plot_joined_forecast.py
def plot_joined_forecast(history_times, history_values, forecast_times,
                         actual_values, forecast_values, target_names):
    """Plot all direct forecasts against their histories and actual outputs."""
    if len(history_times) != history_values.shape[0]:
        raise ValueError("History times and values must have the same length.")
    if len(forecast_times) != actual_values.shape[0]:
        raise ValueError("Forecast times and actual values must have the same length.")
    if len(forecast_times) != forecast_values.shape[0]:
        raise ValueError("Forecast times and values must have the same length.")
    if actual_values.shape != forecast_values.shape:
        raise ValueError("Actual and forecast values must have the same shape.")
    if history_values.shape[1] != actual_values.shape[1]:
        raise ValueError("History and forecast values must have the same targets.")
    if history_values.shape[1] != len(target_names):
        raise ValueError("One target name is required for each target.")

    joined_times = np.concatenate((history_times, forecast_times))
    joined_actual_values = np.concatenate((history_values, actual_values))
    joined_forecast_values = np.concatenate((history_values, forecast_values))
    figure, axes = plt.subplots(len(target_names), 1, figsize=(9, 8),
                                 sharex=True)
    for target_index, (axis, target_name) in enumerate(zip(axes, target_names)):
        axis.plot(joined_times, joined_actual_values[:, target_index],
                  color="black", linewidth=2, label="Observed")
        axis.plot(joined_times, joined_forecast_values[:, target_index],
                  color="tab:green", linewidth=2, label="Direct LSTM")
        axis.axvline(forecast_times[0], color="tab:gray", linestyle="--",
                    label="Forecast begins")
        axis.set_ylabel(target_name)
        axis.grid(alpha=0.3)
        axis.legend(loc="best")
    axes[-1].set_xlabel("Time (h)")
    figure.suptitle("Direct Multi-Output Forecasts Joined to Input History")
    figure.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    return joined_times, joined_actual_values, joined_forecast_values

NoteInterpreting the result

The error at later forecast positions can be larger than the error immediately after the history window. This does not arise from recursively feeding predictions into the model: the direct LSTM predicts every position in one forward pass. Instead, longer-horizon changes can be harder to infer from past measurements alone.

The model does not know an operator’s future heating-input decisions. Boilup is one of the responses it predicts, not a supplied future input. A production forecasting system would need a planned future heating-input trajectory or an explicit assumption about that trajectory. A low test RMSE also does not establish that the model is suitable for control, safety decisions, or operating conditions outside the training data.

Conclusion

This tutorial transformed a dynamic distillation dataset into a direct multi-horizon, multi-output forecasting problem. The manual LSTM cell used basic PyTorch layers and operations to control what information is retained, forgotten, and exposed at each time step. Repeating that cell across a history window produced a final hidden state, and a linear head converted that state directly into 50-point forecasts of boilup, bottoms composition, and distillate composition.

Model element Purpose Limitation
History window Represents recent process state and operating conditions Cannot contain unmeasured disturbances
Manual LSTM cell Learns which information to retain across time Less computationally efficient than nn.LSTM
Direct output head Predicts boilup and both composition trajectories without recursive feedback Trained for one fixed forecast horizon and target set
Persistence baseline Provides a simple, transparent comparison Cannot represent anticipated process dynamics

For an extension, modify the dataset construction so the model also receives a planned future heating-input trajectory. This would turn the model into an input-conditioned process forecaster, which is useful when a future operating plan is known.
